summary: Defines IMAP extensions that improve international support, including language negotiation for error text, translations of namespace prefixes, and comparator negotiation for search, sort, and thread. IMAP4rev1 already handled non-ASCII mailbox names and MIME-encoded content in a basic way. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary:
IMAP is the protocol an email client uses to read mail from a server. This document adds three IMAP extensions for software that has to work in more than one language.

One extension lets the client ask the server to write its error messages and folder prefixes in the user's own language. Two more make search, sorting and threading use rules that understand the language of the text being compared, instead of always matching letters the same way.

questions: how does imap comparator command work
subtitle: IMAP extensions for language negotiation, translated folder prefixes and international search, sort and threading.

tldr.problem: IMAP4rev1 has basic support for non-ASCII mailbox names and search substrings, but server error text is limited to US-ASCII, namespace prefixes cannot be translated, and SEARCH, SORT and THREAD always use plain case-insensitive matching.
tldr.mechanism: The LANGUAGE extension lets the client ask the server to use a chosen language for human-readable text and, with the NAMESPACE extension, for folder prefixes. The I18NLEVEL extensions make search, sort and thread use a comparator from the IANA collation registry, with I18NLEVEL=2 adding a COMPARATOR command to choose one.
tldr.outcome: A server that advertises I18NLEVEL=1 or I18NLEVEL=2 must implement the i;unicode-casemap comparator and must support UTF-8 as a search charset. Clients are told to re-issue LANGUAGE once a security layer is active, and the RFC leaves Unicode logins and UTF-8 mailbox names to other work.

today: RFC 5255 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It adds the LANGUAGE, I18NLEVEL=1 and I18NLEVEL=2 keywords to the IMAP4 Capabilities Registry, and it leaves Unicode logins and UTF-8 mailbox names to other standards work.

sections.title: What This Specification Adds
sections.content:
IMAP version 4rev1, defined in RFC 3501, has basic support for non-ASCII characters in mailbox names and search substrings, and it supports non-ASCII message headers and content encoded as specified by MIME. This specification defines a collection of IMAP extensions that improve international support: language negotiation for international error text, translations for namespace prefixes, and comparator negotiation for search, sort and thread.

The extensions can be advertised and implemented separately. The LANGUAGE extension allows the client to request a suitable language for protocol error messages and, in combination with the NAMESPACE extension of RFC 2342, enables namespace translations.

The I18NLEVEL=2 extension allows the client to request a suitable collation, which modifies the behaviour of the base specification's SEARCH command as well as the SORT and THREAD extensions. It leverages the collation registry of RFC 4790. The I18NLEVEL=1 extension updates SEARCH, SORT and THREAD to use the i;unicode-casemap comparator, as defined in the Unicode collation specification. I18NLEVEL=1 is a simpler version of I18NLEVEL=2, with no ability to select a different collation.
sections.plainLanguage:
IMAP is the protocol an email client uses to read mail from a server. This document adds three IMAP extensions for software that has to work in more than one language.

One extension lets the client ask the server to write its error messages and folder prefixes in the user's own language. Two more make search, sorting and threading use rules that understand the language of the text being compared, instead of always matching letters the same way.

sections.title: The LANGUAGE Command
sections.content:
IMAP allows server responses to include human-readable text that in many cases needs to be presented to the user, but that text is limited to US-ASCII by the IMAP specification in order to preserve backwards compatibility with deployed implementations. The LANGUAGE extension is a way for an IMAP client to negotiate which language the server should use when sending human-readable text.

A server that supports the extension MUST list the keyword LANGUAGE in its CAPABILITY response and in the greeting CAPABILITY data, and it MUST use the language i-default as its default until the client negotiates another supported language. A server SHOULD NOT advertise the extension if it discovers that it only supports i-default. Clients and servers that support the extension MUST also support the NAMESPACE extension.

The LANGUAGE command is valid in all states, and clients SHOULD issue it before authentication, because some servers send useful information as part of authentication. If a security layer such as SASL or TLS is negotiated afterwards, the client MUST re-issue the LANGUAGE command. If the command succeeds, the server returns human-readable responses in the first supported language specified, in UTF-8, and it MUST send a LANGUAGE response naming the language used; the change takes effect immediately after that response. If the command fails, the server continues to use the language it was previously using.

The special default argument asks for a language designated as preferred by the server administrator, and that preference MAY vary based on the currently active user. If a language range does not match a known language tag exactly but does match a language by the rules of RFC 4647, the server MUST send an untagged LANGUAGE response indicating the language selected. If there are no arguments, the server SHOULD send an untagged LANGUAGE response listing the languages it supports, and MAY return a tagged NO response if it cannot enumerate them.

The LANGUAGE response holds a list of one or more language tags. A response with a single tag means the server is now using that language. A response with several tags means the server is listing the languages available to the client, and no change has been made.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a LANGUAGE command with the language it wants, and the server answers with the language it settled on. If the server cannot use any of them, it says so and carries on in the language it was already using. Sending the command with no arguments asks the server which languages it can do.

sections.title: Translations for Namespace Prefixes
sections.content:
If localized representations of the namespace prefixes are available in the selected language, the server SHOULD include these in the TRANSLATION extension to the NAMESPACE response. The TRANSLATION extension returns a single string, containing the modified UTF-7 encoded translation of the namespace prefix. It is the responsibility of the client to convert between the namespace prefix and its translation when presenting mailbox names to the user.

The example in the RFC shows a server that supports the IMAP4 NAMESPACE command, uses no prefix for the user's Personal Namespace, a prefix of Other Users for its Other Users' Namespace, and a prefix of Public Folders for its only Shared Namespace. Since a client will often display these prefixes to the user, the server includes a translation of them that can be presented to the user. In the example, the client asks for German and the server returns Andere Benutzer and Gemeinsame Postfaecher alongside the original prefixes.

The LANGUAGE extension only provides a mechanism for altering fixed server strings such as response text and NAMESPACE folder names. Assigning localized language aliases to shared mailboxes would need a separate mechanism, such as the METADATA extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail servers group folders into named areas, such as a user's own folders, other people's folders and shared folders. The name of each group is often shown to the user. With this extension the server can also send a translated version of that name in the user's chosen language.

sections.title: Two Levels of Comparator Support
sections.content:
The IMAP4rev1 SEARCH command locates messages matching criteria that include human-readable text, and the SORT extension lets the client ask the server to determine the order of messages based on criteria that also include human-readable text. Both need the ability to support non-English search and sort functions. This section defines two IMAP extensions for internationalizing SEARCH, SORT and THREAD using the comparator framework of RFC 4790.

I18NLEVEL=1 updates SEARCH, SORT and THREAD to use the i;unicode-casemap comparator. I18NLEVEL=2 is a superset of it: it adds the ability to determine the active comparator and to negotiate the use of comparators with the COMPARATOR command, and it adds the COMPARATOR response that indicates the active comparator and possibly other available comparators.

Two terms matter here. The default comparator is the one used by SEARCH and SORT when no COMPARATOR command has been used. The active comparator is the one that will be used within the session, for example by SEARCH and SORT; the COMPARATOR command changes it.

The active comparator applies to the SEARCH keys BCC, BODY, CC, FROM, SUBJECT, TEXT, TO and HEADER. If the server also advertises the SORT extension, it applies to the SORT keys CC, FROM, SUBJECT and TO. If the server advertises THREAD=ORDEREDSUBJECT, it applies to the ORDEREDSUBJECT threading algorithm, and if the server advertises THREAD=REFERENCES, it applies to the subject field comparisons done by the REFERENCES threading algorithm. For SORT and THREAD, the pre-processing needed to extract the base subject text from a Subject header happens before the comparator is applied.

A server that advertises I18NLEVEL=1 or I18NLEVEL=2 MUST implement the i;unicode-casemap comparator and MUST support UTF-8 as a SEARCH charset. A server advertising I18NLEVEL=1 MUST list the keyword I18NLEVEL=1 in its CAPABILITY data once IMAP enters the authenticated state; a server advertising I18NLEVEL=2 does the same with I18NLEVEL=2. A server that advertises I18NLEVEL=2 SHOULD use i;unicode-casemap as the default comparator, though the choice MAY be adjustable by the administrator and MAY be sensitive to the current user. Once the connection enters the authenticated state, the default comparator MUST remain static for the rest of that connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A comparator is a named rule for comparing two pieces of text. Level 1 says the server must use one particular comparator, the one that understands Unicode case folding. Level 2 says the same, but also lets the client ask for a different comparator at run time.

sections.title: How a Server Collates Text
sections.content:
RFC 3501 says that in all search keys that use strings, a message matches the key if the string is a substring of the field, and that the matching is case-insensitive. When performing the SEARCH operation, the active comparator is applied instead of that case-insensitive matching.

A server that performs collation operations, as part of commands such as SEARCH, SORT and THREAD, does so in three steps. First, MIME encoding MUST be removed in the texts being collated, for example the header encoding of RFC 2047 and the body part encoding of RFC 2045. If MIME encoding removal fails for a message, the collation of that message is undefined by this specification and is handled in an implementation-dependent manner. Second, the decoded text MUST be converted to the charset expected by the active comparator.

Third, the comparison itself. For the substring operation, if the charset conversion failed, the original decoded text is collated using the i;octet comparator. If it succeeded, the converted text is collated according to the active comparator. If the substring operation of the active comparator returns the undefined result for either the text specified in the command or the message text, the operation is repeated on the result of the first step using the i;octet comparator.

For the ordering operation, all strings that were successfully converted are separated from all strings that failed the conversion, and strings in each group are collated independently. Strings that were converted are then validated by the active comparator; those that pass are collated with the active comparator, and those that either failed the conversion or fail the validity operation are collated with the i;octet comparator. The resulting sorted list is produced by appending all the collated failed strings after all the strings collated using the active comparator. The RFC's worked example orders four strings, and reaches the order (4) (2) (3) (1): the string that converted successfully comes first, and the two that failed validation follow it in i;octet order.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the server can compare two texts it has to make them comparable. It removes any MIME encoding, converts the text into the character set the comparator expects, and then compares. If the conversion fails, the server falls back to comparing raw bytes, and puts those messages after the ones it could compare properly.

sections.title: The COMPARATOR Command
sections.content:
The COMPARATOR command is valid in the authenticated and selected states, and is used to determine or change the active comparator. When issued with no arguments, it results in a COMPARATOR response indicating the currently active comparator. When issued with one or more comparator arguments, it changes the active comparator as directed, and if more than one installed comparator is matched by an argument, the first argument wins. The COMPARATOR response lists all matching comparators if more than one matches the specified patterns.

The argument default refers to the server's default comparator. Otherwise, each argument is a collation specification as defined in the Internet Application Protocol Comparator Registry of RFC 4790. In the RFC's example, the client asks for a Czech comparator if possible, or else a generic international comparator it considers suitable for Czech, and the server picks the first supported comparator, replying with the untagged response COMPARATOR i;basic and the tagged response A001 OK Will use i;basic for collation.

The COMPARATOR response holds the active comparator and an optional list of available matching comparators. Its first argument is the name of the active comparator, and the second argument is a list of comparators which matched any of the arguments to the COMPARATOR command, present only if more than one match is found.

A BADCOMPARATOR response code SHOULD be returned when the server fails an IMAP command with a NO response and knows that none of the specified comparators match the requested ones. Because SEARCH uses the substring operation, an IMAP server can only implement collations that offer the substring operation, and because SORT uses the ordering operation, which in turn uses the equality operation, a server that advertises SORT can only implement collations that offer all three operations. If the active collation does not provide the operations an IMAP command needs, the server MUST respond with a tagged BAD.
sections.plainLanguage: The COMPARATOR command is how a client finds out which comparison rule the server is using, and asks for a different one. The client can ask for a specific rule or for a family of rules and let the server choose the first one it has.

sections.title: Existing Servers and the Default Comparator
sections.content:
Several server implementations deployed before this specification was published comply with I18NLEVEL=1 but do not advertise it. Other legacy servers use the i;ascii-casemap comparator.

There is no good way for a client to know which comparator a legacy server uses. If the client has to assume the worst, it may end up doing expensive local operations to obtain i;unicode-casemap comparisons even though the server implements it.

Legacy server implementations that comply with I18NLEVEL=1 should be updated to advertise I18NLEVEL=1, and all server implementations should eventually be updated to comply with the I18NLEVEL=2 extension.

The RFC also lists internationalization issues this specification does not resolve. IMAP4rev1 restricts the userid and password fields of the LOGIN command to US-ASCII until a future standards track RFC says otherwise, and servers are encouraged to validate both fields against the formal syntax of UTF-8 and to reject the LOGIN command if that syntax is violated. The modified UTF-7 mailbox naming convention is best viewed as a transition from the status quo in 1996, when local character sets such as ISO-8859-1 and Shift-JIS were widely used for non-ASCII mailbox names with resultant non-interoperability; the requirements in Section 5.1 of RFC 3501 are considered very important, and servers are encouraged to enforce them. The RFC also notes that it would be unwise to move forward with work on internationalised domain names in the server until the work in progress on the format of international email addresses is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail servers already behave as if they supported the simpler level of international search, but do not say so, and some still compare text with plain ASCII rules. A client cannot tell which it is talking to, so it may have to do the careful comparison itself. The RFC asks server implementers to start advertising what they already do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The LANGUAGE extension makes a new command available in the Not Authenticated state of IMAP. Some IMAP implementations run with root privilege when the server is in that state and do not revoke that privilege until after authentication is complete. Such implementations are particularly vulnerable to buffer overflow security errors at this stage and need to implement parsing of this command with extra care.

A LANGUAGE command issued before a security layer is activated is subject to an active attack that suppresses or modifies the negotiation, which makes STARTTLS or authentication error messages harder to interpret. This is not a new attack, because the error messages themselves are subject to active attack. Clients MUST re-issue the LANGUAGE command once a security layer is active, in order to prevent this attack from affecting later protocol operations.

The LANGUAGE, I18NLEVEL=1 and I18NLEVEL=2 extensions use the UTF-8 charset, so the security considerations for UTF-8 in RFC 3629 are relevant. However, none of them uses UTF-8 for identifiers, so the most serious of those concerns do not apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The language command can be sent before the client logs in, which is when some servers are still running with the highest privileges. Such servers have to parse the new command carefully. The client also has to send the language command again after the connection is made secure, because an attacker could have interfered with the first one.
